claims.text: Lattice distortion is the primary factor governing hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys.
A random distribution of elements with different atomic radii produces lattice distortion and variations in interatomic distances in high-entropy alloys.
Greater lattice distortion generates stronger internal stress fields.
Internal stress fields generated by lattice distortion impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion caused by lattice distortion enhances hardness and yield strength.
An equiatomic or near-equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi alloy or refractory HEA can serve as a low-lattice-distortion baseline because it has minimal atomic-size mismatch.
Substituting elements to increase atomic-radius mismatch will increase lattice distortion.
Variations in interatomic distances and lattice distortion can be quantified from X-ray diffraction peak broadening.
Local strain fields from larger lattice distortions act as barriers to dislocation motion through solid-solution strengthening.
Alloys with larger atomic-size mismatch and greater lattice distortion will have higher hardness than otherwise comparable baseline alloys.
Alloys with larger atomic-size mismatch and greater lattice distortion will have higher yield strength than otherwise comparable baseline alloys.
A baseline alloy with minimal atomic-size mismatch will have lower lattice distortion, hardness, and strength.
The proposed governing behavior is limited to single-phase, disordered high-entropy alloys without second-phase precipitates or significant phase segregation.
At extreme temperatures or compositions that cause phase separation, strengthening mechanisms other than lattice distortion may dominate.
The relative contributions of precipitation hardening, dislocation interactions, and lattice distortion have not been quantitatively separated.
The quantitative relationship between lattice-distortion magnitude and mechanical-property increases requires further calibration.
